title: Concrete or Pavers? How to Choose for Your Ohio Driveway
excerpt: Both last decades when they are installed right. The decision usually comes down to budget, repairs and the look you want in front of your home.
author: Maxima Concrete

body.text: As a homeowner, you may be wondering about your driveway: should it be poured concrete or pavers? There is no universal answer. Both surfaces can last for decades when the base is properly installed — and both can deteriorate quickly when it is not. What changes is the upfront cost, ease of repairs, and the overall appearance of the driveway from the street.

A poured concrete driveway is a single, continuous slab. It is the more affordable option of the two per square foot, easy to clear in the winter, and, with a 6.5-bag concrete mix, fiber mesh, and 10-gauge wire mesh, it performs well through Ohio’s freeze-thaw cycles. The downside is repairs: because the slab is continuous, repairing a damaged area typically means cutting out and replacing a section, and the patch rarely matches the original color exactly.

A paver driveway offers a significantly more sophisticated look, bringing high-end architecture, rich textures, and custom patterns directly into the landscape. Its main structural advantage is long-term maintenance: if an individual paver becomes stained or damaged, it can be removed and replaced without compromising the rest of the driveway.

To ensure the highest quality, Maxima installs pavers, bricks, and stone over a poured concrete base whenever permitted. Instead of allowing the pavers to shift independently over unstable soil, this advanced method secures them to a rigid structure, allowing them to move uniformly with the concrete base. It is widely considered a best engineering practice for minimizing shifting and settling.

items: Budget: Concrete has a lower upfront installation cost; interlocking pavers represent a higher-end architectural investment but can require fewer ongoing repairs over time.
Repairs: Individual pavers can be removed and replaced; concrete typically needs to be saw-cut, patched, or partially replaced.
Appearance: Concrete offers standard finishes and solid colors; interlocking pavers provide a highly sophisticated look with textured stones, borders, and intricate laying patterns.
Snow: Both concrete options handle snow removal well when properly installed, although standard poured concrete provides a completely uniform surface for shoveling.

body.text: The Part No One Talks About

Regardless of the surface you choose, the base underneath it determines how long it will last. Concrete has very little tolerance for ground movement — if the soil settles, a standard slab can span the void and crack. Traditional pavers, meanwhile, are vulnerable to movement when installed over a gravel base. Using a concrete sub-base provides an ideal structural foundation, helping keep high-quality pavers level and stable for years to come. When comparing estimates, ask what will be installed under the surface, not just what will be installed on it.
